memoryText: For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Job 19:25 is the unit’s anchor verse, and it deserves a final look. Read it aloud once more before you go on.

“For I know.” This is the language of certainty. Job has been saying “I do not understand” for eighteen chapters. Now he says “I know.” The things he does not know are many. What he knows is one thing, and it is enough.

“That my Redeemer lives.” The word for “Redeemer” is the family rescuer, the one who steps in when a relative is in trouble. Job does not say that he hopes for one or that he wishes for one. He says that he has one, and that this person is alive. In the middle of death and loss, he points to life.

“And at the last he will stand upon the earth.” There will be a final day. The Redeemer will take his place on the earth, as a judge or an advocate in a courtroom. The one who seems to be missing will come. The wrongs will be set right.

Job could not have known how fully this would be fulfilled. In Jesus, the Redeemer has come, lived, died, and risen. He lives, and he will stand upon the earth again. Every Christian can say this verse with more confidence than Job, because we have seen the empty tomb. Keep the verse close. It will carry you through the hardest days.
unitRecap:
In Unit 4 you have read the book of Job and a series of psalms that go with it. The unit began with a scene that Job himself never saw: the heavenly court, where Satan accused Job of serving God only for the benefits. God allowed Job to be tested, within limits, and Job lost his children, his wealth, and his health. Even so, he worshiped. You prayed Psalms 10 and 13, which gave you words for “Where are you?” and “How long?”

Then the friends came. Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar each spoke three times, and they all said the same thing in different ways: Job must have sinned. They defended God with false claims, and they turned a general truth about wisdom and consequences into a rule that crushed a suffering man. Job answered them with grief and anger and honesty. Through his speeches, a longing grew: for an arbiter, for a witness in heaven, and for a Redeemer who lives. In chapter 19 he said the words that anchor this unit.

You read Psalm 22, the great psalm of the forsaken and the vindicated, and saw how Jesus prayed it on the cross. In the later chapters, Job insisted on his integrity, praised God’s power as only the outskirts of his ways, and heard the poem on wisdom that ends with the fear of the Lord. Elihu spoke last among the humans, and he said some wise things and some mistaken ones.

Then God answered from the whirlwind. He did not explain, but asked questions about the world he had made. Job saw him, repented of his presumption, and prayed for his friends. God vindicated Job and restored him. In two doctrinal pauses, you studied God’s providence and the Christian’s suffering. In Psalms 73, 88, 17, and 26, you found a sanctuary where the truth comes back into focus, a prayer for the darkest night, the hope of seeing God’s face, and a plea for redemption.

The unit taught that suffering is not a verdict, that God is sovereign and good, and that the answer to suffering is not an explanation but a Person.

reviewQuestions.question: What does the prologue of Job reveal about the nature of suffering and Satan’s role?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look back at chapters 1 and 2. Satan can act only with God’s permission, and every time the permission has a limit. Job’s suffering was not punishment, and he never learned the reason. What does this teach you about how to think about suffering in your own life? How does it help you to know that Satan is on a leash?

reviewQuestions.question: Where do Job’s friends go wrong in their theology of suffering?
reviewQuestions.prompt: The friends held a general truth, that sin has consequences, and turned it into a rule that explained everything. Recall how they treated Job, and how God responded in 42:7. What lessons about comforting people and handling Scripture do you take from their mistakes? Is there a place where you are tempted to do what they did?

reviewQuestions.question: How does God’s answer from the whirlwind address Job’s questions?
reviewQuestions.prompt: God did not give Job an explanation. He asked questions about creation, and showed Job his own wisdom and care. Job’s response was, “Now my eye sees you.” Why was that enough? Write a few sentences about what it means that the answer to suffering is God himself.

reviewQuestions.question: How does Job’s story point forward to Christ, the truly righteous one who suffered?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Think about Job’s longing for a mediator, a witness, and a Redeemer, and about Psalm 22. Jesus is the righteous one who suffered unjustly, the mediator who stands between God and us, and the Redeemer who lives. Write a short prayer of thanks to him for each of these roles.

prayerPrompts: Thank God that suffering is never a sign he has left you.
Ask him to help you trust him when you do not understand.
Ask him to prepare you for what comes next.
